source: General Directorate of Agriculture (GDA), Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, Cambodia — Sweet Corn Production Handbook (ផលិតកម្មដំណំពោតផ្អែម), Appendix 7 'Guide to identifying corn nutrient deficiency symptoms', in partnership with SNV
text:
The handbook's appendix includes a visual diagnostic key for identifying which nutrient a corn plant is lacking, based on where discoloration/symptoms first appear on the plant (older/lower leaves vs. younger/upper leaves) and the color pattern observed. Because this section was rendered as a diagram/branching chart with dense Khmer text, the following summarizes the general branch logic verified against the page images; some individual nutrient labels in the diagram were difficult to read with full confidence and are flagged as such below.

General stunting with no clear discoloration pattern typically indicates a general/multiple nutrient deficiency.

When older (lower) leaves show discoloration first:
1. Yellowing starting from the leaf tip and moving inward in a V-shaped pattern along the midrib of the leaf, on the upper/older leaves — indicates Nitrogen (អាសូត) deficiency.
2. Reddish-purple color and drying along the outer leaf margin from tip toward the base — indicates a deficiency the source labels as related to Potassium (this label was harder to read with full confidence from the scanned diagram).
3. Color change on the leaf midrib/margin area with drying from tip to base — labeled as Magnesium (ម៉ាញ៉ែស្យូម) deficiency in the source.
4. Purple/violet discoloration and drying from tip backward, with stunted growth — labeled as Phosphorus (ផូស្វ័រ) deficiency.

When younger (upper) leaves show discoloration first:
1. New leaves emerge pale yellow, particularly toward the base of the leaf — labeled as Zinc (ស័ង្កសី) deficiency.
2. Leaves show fine interveinal striping running the length of the leaf — labeled as Iron (ជាតិដែក) deficiency.
3. Young leaves show pale yellow streaking between veins, with older leaf tips dying — labeled as Copper (ទង់ដែង) deficiency.
4. White or irregular discoloration between the leaf vein and blade — labeled as Boron (បូរ៉ុន) deficiency.
5. Young leaves show streaking that develops into pale coloring between vein and blade — labeled as Manganese deficiency in the source.
6. Leaves appear scorched/burnt and die along the margin — labeled as Molybdenum deficiency in the source.
7. Normally young leaves resemble older leaves in appearance, but symptoms can appear as raised bumps/nodules between vein and blade — labeled as Calcium (ការខ្វះកាល់ស្យូម) deficiency, described elsewhere in the appendix as related to soil pH below about 5.2.

Detailed narrative descriptions given for individual nutrients (matched to their photo captions):

Phosphorus (ផូស្វ័រ) deficiency: leaves may appear darker/more purple than a normal plant, with purple discoloration first appearing on the underside of the leaf near the base, later spreading over the whole plant. Growth is slowed, the plant stays small and short, and maturity is delayed. Symptoms are especially pronounced when the plant experiences excess soil water.

Potassium deficiency: first appears as yellowing at the tips of the lower/older leaves, developing along the outer leaf margin as yellow then light brown then darker brown discoloration, while the inner leaf area stays green; the affected area can eventually spread across the whole leaf. Deficient plants appear weak and stunted, and kernels at the ear tip are shriveled and do not fill out completely.

Sulfur (ស្តាន់ធ័រ) deficiency: pale yellow-green striping appears along the length of young leaves near the top of the plant, similar in appearance to Nitrogen deficiency, but Sulfur deficiency shows first on the newest/uppermost leaves rather than the older ones.

Molybdenum (ម៉ូលីប្តេណូស) deficiency: symptoms appear on the newest, most recently emerged leaves, similar in pattern to Iron deficiency. Molybdenum deficiency tends to occur on soils with pH around 6.0-6.3, whereas Iron deficiency is more associated with soils with pH around 6.5 or higher.

Magnesium deficiency: older leaves show a weakened, wilted appearance, with new leaves remaining green while older leaves near the base turn yellow/discolored. This is commonly associated with acidic soils (pH below about 5.2), similar to Aluminum toxicity symptoms, and often co-occurs with Manganese excess.

Iron deficiency: shows as pale interveinal striping on the newest leaves at the top of the plant, while older lower leaves stay green; associated with soils having pH around 7.0 or higher; not typically linked to a shortage of Phosphorus, Copper, Manganese, or Zinc, and tends to be worse in poorly aerated soil.

(Note: the pest/disease-vs-growth-stage cross-reference table in Appendix 6, listing symptom categories such as physiological, disease, insect, and other causes across germination and vegetative growth stages, was also visually checked; it lists conditions such as poor germination, seedling rot, stem/root rot, seedling wilt, herbicide (2,4-D) injury, and various insect and disease causes, but several individual table cells were too terse or ambiguous in the source to translate reliably and have been omitted here rather than guessed.)
